summary:
Guadeloupe stands under France's national framework. The Penal Code that decriminalised same-sex relations in 1791 and was retained in the 1810 Code applies here, as do the anti-discrimination statutes, the marriage regime and the rules on identity documents. No legal penalty attaches to being trans, and same-sex marriage is available on the same terms as in mainland France.

Hate-motivated conduct is criminalised. The law of 31 December 2004 penalises injury, defamation, insult and incitement to hatred, violence or discrimination on grounds including gender and sexual orientation, with a maximum of a 45,000 euro fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment. Conversion therapy carries up to two years' imprisonment and/or a 30,000 euro fine under legislation published on 1 February 2022. A 2020 government report recorded a 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in 2019, with police identifying roughly 1,870 victims against about 1,380 the previous year.

Legal gender recognition has been available without surgery or medical diagnosis since 1 January 2017 under the statute signed on 18 November 2016. A change of gender marker still requires an appearance before a court, while a first-name change can be completed at the registry office. Self-certification of gender and proof of medical treatment were both dropped from the final text. A 2017 bid to introduce a 'neutral sex' classification was rejected by the Court of Cassation.

Custodial settings are the documented risk area. A BuzzFeed News report of January 2018 found that in the French prison system, which governs detention in Guadeloupe, the placement of trans women follows the legal gender recorded on the incarceration papers, which may not correspond to the person's presentation; in practice, assignment is said to weigh the individual's best interests, with individual cells or placement in more welcoming wings used where possible. The national preventive mechanism, the CGLPL, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding that serious violations of the fundamental rights of transgender detainees persist across places of deprivation of liberty, drawing on some 40 referrals it had received since 2010.

Gender-affirming care is funded through the Sécurité Sociale's long-term illness scheme, ALD 31, and surgery has been legal domestically since 1979. Access remains uneven. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report documented deficits in self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, and recommended an informed-consent model. The French Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and advised extreme caution on access, though this did not alter practice.

Trans minors are a live legislative target. In March 2024 centre-right senators commissioned a report from the Little Mermaid Observatory, a body opposed to all gender transition for minors, which described transition as a 'health scandal'. A bill banning medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, opposed by the Macron government, and has had no recorded movement since 23 July 2024. In late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first trans youth clinical guidelines, recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2.

Community infrastructure on the island has expanded. The Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion, Guadeloupe's first LGBT+ centre, opened on 24 April 2024, offering reception, support and orientation for people of diverse identity, sexual, bodily and gender diversities; it was driven by a federation of Guadeloupean associations and visited by a national government minister, who announced measures to strengthen the fight against gender-based violence and discrimination with structures adapted to overseas territories. Reporting from September 2023 describes community members increasingly reconciling their lives with their identities, with activism advancing after the sister island of Martinique. In 2025 the organisations Secret's Out, Queer Gang and Lovo Nova partnered on a year of LGBT-friendly social events across Guadeloupe.
tangentialFactors:
The national legal position and its contested politics reach Guadeloupe unchanged. The May 2024 Senate bill on under-18 medical transition prompted large-scale protests in France, and the Académie Nationale de Médecine's cautionary framing of treatment demand signals institutional scepticism that visitors may encounter in clinical settings. In 2022 it emerged that the president of the scientific committee of DILCRAH, the national interministerial body against racism, anti-Semitism and anti-LGBT hatred, sat on the Little Mermaid Observatory; one member resigned and the president stepped away from the role.

Family-law recognition has moved through the courts rather than by statute. The Court of Cassation ruled on 5 July 2017 that a child born to a surrogate abroad could be adopted by the partner of the biological father, the Paris Court of Appeal recognised a Canadian birth certificate in May 2019, and in December 2019 the Court of Cassation held that foreign birth certificates recognising same-sex partners must be fully recognised in France. In 2022 a court of appeal ruled that a transgender woman should be regarded as the mother of the child she had conceived before her sex change.

Administrative guidance exists for institutions. In March 2019 the higher education minister announced that all higher education institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms. In January 2019 the Ministry of Education launched the campaign 'Tous égaux, tous alliés' against anti-LGBTQ bullying, with reporting services, a helpline for students and staff, guidance obligations for schools and 17 May as a designated sensitisation day.
localsOnly:
Residents fund and run the support infrastructure. The Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion was created by a federation of Guadeloupean associations and operates as a reception, support and orientation point, so the practical route to services runs through local associations rather than a national agency. Secret's Out, Queer Gang and Lovo Nova organised a shared calendar of LGBT-friendly social activity across the island during 2025.

Gender-affirming medical care for residents is accessed through ALD 31, the Sécurité Sociale long-term illness category, which covers treatment costs; access to surgical and endocrine services depends on referral routes and availability, which a 2022 ILGA-Europe review found to be geographically uneven nationally. Blood donation deferrals for gay and bi men were reduced to four months in April 2020 and abolished entirely on 16 March 2022. School enrolment forms use 'parent 1' and 'parent 2', a usage that drew national political contestation in February 2019.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Guadeloupe-specific enforcement data is available in the sources reviewed. There are no recorded figures for hate-crime incidents on the island, no caseload data for legal gender recognition petitions filed in Guadeloupe, and no breakdown showing where the CGLPL's roughly 40 transgender-detention referrals since 2010 were made, so the national findings cannot be attributed to any particular Guadeloupean facility. The January 2018 account of prison placement practice is drawn from national reporting and describes a practice said to inform individual decisions rather than a written rule.

Availability of gender-affirming care within Guadeloupe itself is unresolved. The sources document national funding and national access problems but do not state which services, if any, are provided on the island, and a visitor needing care would have to establish this locally or travel. The status of the Senate bill on medical transition for under-18s has not been updated since 23 July 2024, and the national compensation bill for men prosecuted under the repealed 1960 indecent-exposure enhancement was passed by the National Assembly in March 2024 without a recorded Senate vote.
